C. The model does not support the Converse API

D. Cached input tokens are billed at the standard rate

Correct: A. Caching only pays when the same prefix repeats within the TTL. With 30-minute gaps and a ~5-minute TTL, every call misses: each pays full recomputation plus the write surcharge, which can cost more than no caching at all.

B is wrong: 6,000 tokens exceeds the minimum prefix thresholds. C is wrong: the issue is call spacing, not API support. Converse supports cache points on caching-capable models. D is wrong: cached input tokens are billed at a discounted rate; the problem is that no calls are hitting the cache.

MREasy Which TWO are requirements for prompt caching to work? (Select TWO)

A. The model must support caching (e.g. Claude 3.5+, Nova)

B. The cached prefix must meet the minimum token threshold

C. The workload must use batch inference

D. The application must run on EC2

E. Temperature must be set to 0

Correct: A, B. Caching is a model capability (not all models implement it) and requires a minimum prefix length before the cache point.

C is wrong: caching applies to real-time invocations, not batch jobs. D is wrong: the compute platform is irrelevant. E is wrong: temperature is unrelated to caching.

MRMedium A company uses the Converse API with a 12,000-token system prompt that changes weekly. Which TWO statements about applying prompt caching are true? (Select TWO)

A. Add a cachePoint after the system prompt content so it is treated as the cached prefix

B. Cached input tokens are billed at a discounted rate versus standard input tokens

C. The cache persists indefinitely once written

D. Caching also discounts output tokens

E. Changing the system prompt weekly has no effect on the cache

Correct: A, B. A is the Converse mechanism (cachePoint marks the prefix); B is the pricing benefit.

C is wrong: cache entries expire after the TTL (minutes to about an hour). D is wrong: only input tokens before the cache point are discounted. Output tokens are always full price. E is wrong: any prefix change invalidates the cache; after the weekly change, the first calls re-pay the full write.

MRHard An application is throttled at peak AND has a repeated 8,000-token prefix. Which TWO actions together form the most correct response? (Select TWO)

A. Add prompt caching for the repeated prefix to cut input-token cost

B. Add provisioned throughput for the steady baseline to guarantee capacity

C. Switch the interactive workload to batch inference

D. Remove the cache point to reduce latency

E. Increase temperature to reduce throttling

Correct: A, B. Two distinct problems need two levers: caching attacks the repeated-prefix cost, PT attacks the capacity shortfall. This is the exam's favorite "match each lever to its constraint" shape.

C is wrong: batch has hours of latency; the workload is interactive. D is wrong: removing the cache point raises cost and does not help throttling. E is wrong: temperature controls randomness, not capacity.

Questions: Topic 03, Batch inference

MCEasy A media company must classify 500,000 archived support tickets. Results are needed within 24 hours. What is the most cost-effective approach?

A. On-demand inference with a large Lambda fleet

B. Batch inference with S3 input and output

C. Provisioned Throughput for one month

D. Real-time streaming inference

Correct: B. Offline, latency-tolerant, high-volume: batch inference at roughly 50% off on-demand is the designed answer.

A is wrong: full on-demand price plus the operational overhead of a fleet. C is wrong: a one-month hourly commit for a finite job wastes idle hours. D is wrong: streaming optimizes perceived latency for interactive users. There is no user here.

MCMedium A batch inference job finished but 2% of records have errors in the output file. The input was a JSONL file with 100,000 lines. What is the most likely cause and the right next step?

A. The model is overloaded; request a quota increase and rerun everything

B. Individual input lines were malformed; fix those lines and resubmit only them

C. S3 eventual consistency corrupted the output; wait and re-read

D. The IAM role expired mid-job; recreate the role and rerun everything

Correct: B. Batch jobs process lines independently and record per-line errors in the output. A small error fraction points to malformed input lines, not systemic failure; resubmitting just the bad lines is the efficient fix.

A is wrong: batch jobs do not throttle like on-demand; a 2% line-error rate is not capacity. C is wrong: S3 read-after-write is consistent. This does not produce per-line errors. D is wrong: an expired role would fail the whole job, not 2% of lines.

MCHard A team wants to cut costs for a real-time fraud-scoring API (p99 latency requirement: 800ms) by moving it to batch inference. The proposal claims 50% savings. Why is this wrong?

A. Batch inference costs more than on-demand for small jobs

B. Batch inference has hours-scale latency with no SLA, violating the 800ms requirement

C. Fraud scoring models are not supported in batch mode

D. Batch inference cannot read from S3

Correct: B. The latency requirement disqualifies batch entirely. Cost savings are irrelevant when the architecture cannot meet the SLA. This is the exam's core batch trap: a real discount applied to the wrong workload.

A is wrong: batch is cheaper per token regardless of job size. C is wrong: batch supports the same models as on-demand invocation. D is wrong: S3 input is exactly how batch jobs are submitted.

MREasy Which TWO describe batch inference? (Select TWO)

A. Input is a JSONL file in S3; output is written to S3

B. It costs roughly 50% less than on-demand for the same model

C. It guarantees sub-second responses

D. It requires provisioned throughput

E. It processes requests synchronously

Correct: A, B. S3 in and S3 out with async processing is the mechanism; the ~50% discount is the reason to use it.

C is wrong: latency is hours-scale with no SLA. D is wrong: batch needs no reserved capacity. E is wrong: it is asynchronous by design.

MRMedium A nightly ETL job uses batch inference. Which TWO are true about its IAM and data setup? (Select TWO)

A. An IAM role must grant Bedrock read access to the input S3 location

B. An IAM role must grant Bedrock write access to the output S3 location

C. The input file must be uploaded via the Converse API

D. Results are returned in the API response body

E. The job requires a VPC endpoint to reach S3

Correct: A, B. Bedrock acts with the provided role: it must read the input and write the output.

C is wrong: input is a file in S3, not an API payload. D is wrong: results land in S3 as JSONL. Nothing returns synchronously. E is wrong: no VPC endpoint is required for the basic S3-based flow.

MRHard A company runs both an interactive chatbot and a nightly document-summarization job. Which TWO choices form the most cost-effective architecture? (Select TWO)

A. Batch inference for the nightly summarization job

B. On-demand or provisioned throughput for the interactive chatbot, depending on traffic shape

C. Batch inference for the interactive chatbot to halve its cost

D. Provisioned throughput for the nightly job to guarantee it finishes

E. A single pricing model for both workloads to simplify billing

Correct: A, B. Each workload gets the lever matching its latency constraint: batch for offline, real-time capacity for interactive. This is the portfolio answer.

C is wrong: batch latency breaks interactivity. D is wrong: PT commits hourly for a finite nightly job, wasting idle hours. Batch already handles it cheaper. E is wrong: one lever for two different constraints is exactly what the exam punishes.

Questions: Topic 04, Provisioned Throughput

MCEasy An application serves a steady 2M requests per day with a sub-3-second latency SLA. Traffic is predictable. Which option best meets the SLA while controlling cost?

A. On-demand inference only

B. Provisioned Throughput for the baseline plus on-demand for peaks

C. Batch inference

D. A larger model on on-demand

Correct: B. The hybrid is the exam's canonical production answer: reserved capacity guarantees the baseline's latency, on-demand absorbs peaks without paying for idle peak capacity.

A is wrong: shared on-demand capacity can throttle at peak and latency varies. C is wrong: hours of latency violates the SLA. D is wrong: a larger model is slower and pricier per token. It addresses neither capacity nor cost.

MCMedium A team purchased Provisioned Throughput but CloudWatch still shows InvocationThrottles on the base model ID, and the provisioned model shows near-zero invocations. What is wrong?

A. They need more model units

B. The application still invokes the base model ID instead of the provisioned model ARN

C. Provisioned Throughput does not cover throttling

D. The commitment term has expired

Correct: B. The classic routing bug: buying capacity does nothing until invocations target the provisioned model ARN. The near-zero invocations on the provisioned model prove the traffic is going elsewhere.

A is wrong: adding units to an unused reservation fixes nothing. C is wrong: PT's purpose is exactly to avoid on-demand throttling for routed traffic. D is wrong: an expired term would show errors on the provisioned ARN, not zero usage.

MCHard Traffic analysis shows: midnight to 6am near zero, business hours steady at 300 RPM, Friday 2pm to 6pm spikes to 2,000 RPM. The team proposes provisioned throughput sized for 2,000 RPM on a 6-month term to "never throttle." What is the most correct critique?

A. The proposal is optimal because it eliminates all throttling risk

B. Sizing PT for the spike wastes the hourly fee during 90% of hours; provision for the ~300 RPM baseline and let on-demand plus retries absorb spikes

C. Provisioned throughput cannot handle 2,000 RPM

D. They should use batch inference for the Friday spike

Correct: B. PT bills 24/7. Reserving 2,000 RPM of capacity for a 4-hour weekly spike means paying peak prices for ~164 idle hours a week. The cost-correct design provisions the floor and overflows the spike.

A is wrong: "never throttle" is not free; the idle cost dominates. C is wrong: PT can be sized to 2,000 RPM. The issue is economics, not capability. D is wrong: the Friday spike is interactive traffic; batch latency is unacceptable.

MREasy Which TWO statements about Provisioned Throughput are true? (Select TWO)

A. You pay an hourly rate per model unit for the commitment term, used or not

B. Invocations must target the provisioned model ARN to use the reserved capacity

C. It is the cheapest option for spiky, unpredictable traffic

D. It discounts per-token rates on the on-demand pool

E. No commitment term is required

Correct: A, B. The hourly commit regardless of use, and the routing requirement, are the two defining mechanics.

C is wrong: idle hours make PT expensive for spiky traffic. D is wrong: PT is separate reserved capacity, not a discount on on-demand tokens. E is wrong: 1-month or 6-month terms are the commitment mechanism.

MRMedium A steady-state API grows 10% per month. Which TWO features help provisioned throughput handle the growth without manual resizing? (Select TWO)

A. Autoscaling policies that add model units when utilization crosses a threshold

B. Minimum and maximum unit bounds on the scaling policy

C. Switching the workload to batch inference

D. Deleting and recreating the provisioned model daily

E. Raising the temperature to increase throughput

Correct: A, B. Autoscaling adjusts units to utilization; min/max bounds keep cost and capacity within planned limits.

C is wrong: batch changes latency characteristics; it does not scale reserved capacity. D is wrong: daily recreation defeats the commitment and adds churn. E is wrong: temperature affects randomness, not throughput.

MRHard After a model version upgrade, the team reports higher p99 latency on their provisioned throughput setup, but no throttling. Which TWO are plausible causes to investigate? (Select TWO)

A. The new model version is slower per token, so the same unit count delivers less throughput

B. The application was accidentally pointed back at the base model ID

C. Prompt caching was disabled, increasing input processing time

D. The commitment term is too short

E. Batch inference pricing changed

Correct: A, C. A: model units are capacity for a specific model; a slower model version reduces effective throughput per unit. C: losing the cached prefix forces full prefix recomputation, raising time to first token.

B is wrong: pointing at the base model ID would show throttling on the on-demand pool, but the scenario says no throttling. D is wrong: term length affects price, not latency. E is wrong: batch pricing is unrelated to PT latency.

Questions: Topic 05, Inference profiles and routing

MCEasy A model is available in only two regions. The application needs automatic failover if one region throttles or has an outage, with minimal code changes. What should the application call?

A. The bare model ID in a single region

B. The inference profile ID (e.g. with a us. prefix)

C. A provisioned throughput ARN in one region

D. The batch inference API

Correct: B. Inference profiles route across regions in the profile and fail over automatically: the designed answer for regional resilience with minimal code.

A is wrong: a bare model ID pins the app to one region with no failover. C is wrong: PT reserves capacity in one region. It does not fail over. D is wrong: batch is offline and hours-scale.

MCMedium A healthcare application must keep all inference data inside the EU. Which inference profile prefix is appropriate?

A. global.

B. eu.

C. us.

D. apac.

Correct: B. The eu. prefix constrains routing to EU regions, satisfying the data-residency requirement.

A is wrong: global. can route anywhere, violating the constraint. C and D are wrong: they route to the wrong geographies entirely.

MCHard A team confuses three routing features. Their goal: send simple customer queries to a cheap model and complex ones to a flagship model to cut cost. Which feature should they use?

A. An inference profile with a us. prefix

B. A prompt router (model router)

C. Provisioned Throughput

D. Cross-region replication

Correct: B. Routing by prompt complexity for cost and quality is the prompt router's job. This is the exam's three-way confusion set: profiles route by region for availability, routers route by complexity for cost, PT reserves capacity.

A is wrong: inference profiles route across regions, not across model sizes. C is wrong: PT reserves capacity for one model. It does not split traffic by complexity. D is wrong: replication is a data concept, not a Bedrock routing feature.

MREasy Which TWO statements about inference profiles are true? (Select TWO)

A. They route requests across regions for availability and failover

B. The application calls the profile ID instead of the bare model ID

C. They reduce per-token prices

D. They replace provisioned throughput

E. They require a 6-month commitment

Correct: A, B. Cross-region routing with automatic failover is the mechanism; calling the profile ID is how you opt in.

C is wrong: profiles are a routing feature, not a pricing feature. D is wrong: PT is reserved capacity, a different mechanism for a different problem. E is wrong: no commitment is involved.

MRMedium An app hits per-region quotas during a product launch. Which TWO approaches increase effective capacity without rewriting the application? (Select TWO)

A. Call an inference profile so Bedrock pools capacity across regions

B. Request a quota increase from AWS Support

C. Move the launch traffic to batch inference

D. Disable SDK retries to reduce request volume

E. Increase the model temperature

Correct: A, B. A pools regional capacity transparently; B raises the ceiling. Both avoid application rewrites.

C is wrong: a launch is interactive; batch latency is unacceptable. D is wrong: disabling retries turns transient throttles into user-facing errors. E is wrong: temperature is unrelated to capacity.

MRHard A global application needs BOTH regional failover AND cost-based routing between a cheap and a flagship model. Which TWO combine correctly? (Select TWO)

A. A prompt router that selects the model by complexity, with each model invoked via its inference profile for regional failover

B. An inference profile alone, because it also routes by complexity

C. Provisioned throughput alone, because it covers both needs

D. Prompt router for cost routing plus inference profiles for availability routing

E. Batch inference for both workloads

Correct: A, D. Both describe the same correct composition: the router picks which model (cost axis), the profile routes where it runs (availability axis). A and D are two wordings of one architecture.

B is wrong: profiles do not route by complexity. C is wrong: PT reserves capacity; it does neither complexity routing nor regional failover. E is wrong: batch is offline-only.

Questions: Topic 06, Latency, throughput, streaming

MCEasy Users complain a chatbot "feels slow" because answers take 10 seconds to appear, though answers are correct. What is the first change to make?

A. Enable streaming with ConverseStream so tokens render incrementally

B. Buy provisioned throughput

C. Switch to batch inference

D. Add more few-shot examples to the prompt

Correct: A. "Feels slow" with correct answers is a perceived-latency problem. Streaming cuts time to first token, which is what users feel.

B is wrong: PT fixes capacity variance, not the blank-screen wait. C is wrong: batch is slower, the opposite direction. D is wrong: longer prompts increase time to first token.

MCMedium A team streams model output through API Gateway to web clients. Very long responses intermittently cut off. What is the most likely cause?

A. The model stopped generating

B. API Gateway payload and timeout limits on long streaming connections

C. Prompt caching expired mid-stream

D. The temperature is too high

Correct: B. API Gateway imposes payload and timeout limits that make it the wrong carrier for very long streams; the exam tests this explicitly. The fix is WebSockets or direct streaming.

A is wrong: the model generates fine; the transport drops. C is wrong: caching affects input processing, not stream continuity. D is wrong: temperature affects content randomness, not connection lifetime.

MCHard An application has a hard SLA: complete responses in under 3 seconds, p99. Responses average 250 tokens. Which combination is most correct?

A. Streaming alone

B. A smaller, faster model plus provisioned throughput for the steady baseline, with streaming for perceived latency

C. Batch inference with a priority flag

D. Prompt caching alone

Correct: B. A hard complete-response SLA needs actual speed (smaller model), guaranteed capacity without queueing (PT), and streaming helps perception on top. Each piece addresses one sub-constraint.

A is wrong: streaming improves perception but does not guarantee total time. C is wrong: batch has no latency SLA at all. D is wrong: caching trims input processing only. It cannot guarantee a 250-token generation finishes in 3 seconds.

MREasy Which TWO statements about streaming are true? (Select TWO)

A. It reduces time to first token as perceived by the user

B. It changes the total generation time of the response

C. It uses ConverseStream or InvokeModelWithResponseStream

D. It reduces the number of billed tokens

E. It works for batch inference jobs

Correct: A, C. Streaming delivers tokens incrementally (perceived speed) via the streaming API variants.

B is wrong: total generation time is unchanged. D is wrong: token counts and billing are identical. E is wrong: batch jobs write results to S3; there is no live consumer to stream to.

MRMedium A voice assistant needs the lowest possible time to first token. Which TWO levers directly reduce TTFT? (Select TWO)

A. A smaller model with faster per-token generation

B. Prompt caching so the static prefix is not recomputed

C. Raising maxTokens

D. Switching from streaming to non-streaming

E. Adding provisioned throughput during idle periods only

Correct: A, B. A reduces processing time per token including the first; B skips prefix recomputation, which is pure TTFT.

C is wrong: maxTokens affects total length, not the first token. D is wrong: non-streaming delays first visible token until completion. E is wrong: PT during idle periods addresses nothing. And PT reduces queueing variance, not compute time.

MRHard Two teams debate latency fixes. Team X says "streaming makes the model faster." Team Y says "provisioned throughput makes responses more consistent." Which TWO corrections are accurate? (Select TWO)

A. Streaming does not change generation speed; it changes when output becomes visible

B. Provisioned throughput stabilizes capacity and latency variance, not output randomness

C. Streaming reduces p99 total latency by 50%

D. Provisioned throughput makes outputs deterministic across runs

E. Both claims are correct as stated

Correct: A, B. A corrects the streaming misconception; B corrects the PT misconception (consistency of outputs is a temperature and prompt matter, not a capacity matter).

C is wrong: streaming does not reduce total latency at all. D is wrong: PT has no effect on sampling randomness. E is wrong: both claims conflate the mechanism with a different benefit.

Questions: Topic 07, Rate limits, quotas, retries

MCEasy During brief traffic spikes, an application receives ThrottlingException errors. Spikes last under a minute. What is the minimal correct fix?

A. Purchase provisioned throughput

B. Rely on SDK retries with exponential backoff and jitter

C. Request a permanent quota increase

D. Catch the exception and drop the request

Correct: B. Sub-minute spikes are transient; backoff retries absorb them with no architecture change. This is the default SDK behavior.

A is wrong: a 24/7 hourly commit for sub-minute spikes is massive overkill. C is wrong: quota increases are for sustained growth, not transient bursts. D is wrong: dropping requests creates user-facing failures.

MCMedium A developer writes custom retry logic that immediately retries failed requests with no delay. Throttling gets worse during spikes. Why?

A. The model is too slow

B. Immediate retries re-hit the quota gate and can cause retry storms; backoff with jitter is required

C. The IAM role lacks retry permissions

D. CloudWatch metrics are delayed

Correct: B. Retrying instantly adds load to an already-saturated gate. Exponential backoff spreads retries over time; jitter prevents synchronized retry waves.

A is wrong: model speed is unrelated to quota exhaustion. C is wrong: there is no such IAM permission; retries are client behavior. D is wrong: metric delay does not cause throttling.

MCHard An application retries all Bedrock errors including ValidationException up to 5 times. The team notices quota consumption rising with no user benefit. What should change?

A. Increase retries to 10 for all errors

B. Retry only retryable errors (throttling, transient 5xx); fail fast on validation errors

C. Disable all retries

D. Switch to a larger model

Correct: B. Validation errors (malformed request bodies) fail identically on every retry, burning quota for nothing. Retries must be selective.

A is wrong: more retries on hopeless errors wastes more quota. C is wrong: disabling all retries turns transient throttles into user errors. D is wrong: model size is unrelated to request validation.

MREasy Which TWO are true about throttling? (Select TWO)

A. It is AWS deliberately rejecting requests above the quota to protect shared capacity

B. It indicates the request body was malformed

C. Brief throttling is normally absorbed by retries with backoff

D. It only happens on provisioned throughput

E. It means the model is unavailable in the region

Correct: A, C. Throttling is a rate signal, not a bug; transient episodes are the retry use case.

B is wrong: malformed bodies produce validation errors, not throttles. D is wrong: throttling applies to on-demand quotas. PT exists to avoid it. E is wrong: unavailability is an access or regional error, a different failure.

MRMedium A public API fronts Bedrock through API Gateway. Which TWO help protect the backend from client bursts? (Select TWO)

A. API Gateway throttling with per-method rate limits and usage plans

B. SDK exponential backoff with jitter on the backend Bedrock calls

C. Disabling CloudWatch alarms

D. Returning cached responses for identical requests

E. Increasing the model context window

Correct: A, B. A sheds excess load at the edge before it reaches Bedrock; B makes the backend resilient to the throttles that remain.

C is wrong: alarms are observability; disabling them blinds the team. D is a cost optimization, not burst protection (and only helps for identical requests). E is wrong: context window is unrelated to request rates.

MRHard Sustained overload (hours) keeps triggering throttles despite correct retries. Which TWO are appropriate structural responses? (Select TWO)

A. Provisioned throughput sized for the sustained baseline

B. Disable SDK retries to reduce the number of API calls

C. More aggressive immediate retries

D. Requesting a quota increase from AWS Support

E. Reducing the retry backoff to zero

Correct: A, D. Sustained overload is a capacity problem, not a retry problem: reserve dedicated capacity for the baseline or raise the quota ceiling. Retries handle transient spikes; they cannot fix hours of overload.

B is wrong: disabling retries turns transient throttles into user-facing errors. C is wrong: aggressive retries worsen sustained overload. E is wrong: zero backoff creates retry storms.

Questions: Topic 08, Right-sizing and cascading

MCEasy Analysis shows 80% of requests are simple FAQ lookups served by an expensive flagship model, with no quality difference when a lightweight model answers them. What is the most cost-effective change?

A. Fine-tune the flagship model

B. Route simple queries to the lightweight model and keep complex ones on the flagship

C. Enable prompt caching

D. Buy provisioned throughput for the flagship

Correct: B. The workload is bimodal and the small model already matches quality on simple work: cascading captures ~10x per-token savings on 80% of traffic.

A is wrong: fine-tuning is for baked-in behavior, not for a cost problem with an already-working small model. C is wrong: caching helps only with repeated prefixes, not model choice. D is wrong: PT is capacity, not cost reduction.

MCMedium A team builds a cascade with a router model that costs as much per call as the flagship model. What is wrong with this design?

A. Nothing; routers are always worth it

B. The router's cost can erase the savings; the router must be nearly free relative to the calls it routes

C. Cascades require provisioned throughput

D. The flagship model cannot receive routed traffic

Correct: B. Every request pays the router cost plus one model call. An expensive router defeats the purpose; use rules, a tiny model, or the managed prompt router.

A is wrong: router economics must be checked. C is wrong: cascading works on on-demand. D is wrong: routed traffic is ordinary invocations.

MCHard After deploying a cascade, costs fell 60% but user complaints rose on complex queries. Metrics show the router sends 95% of traffic to the small model, including questions the small model answers poorly. What is the fix?

A. Remove the cascade and return to the flagship for everything

B. Tune the router's classification criteria and monitor per-route quality; add low-confidence escalation to the flagship

C. Increase the small model's temperature

D. Enable prompt caching on the flagship

Correct: B. The router misclassifies: the fix is better routing criteria plus a confidence-based escalation path, measured per route. Routing is an optimization loop.

A is wrong: it throws away the 60% saving instead of fixing the classifier. C is wrong: temperature does not fix capability mismatch. D is wrong: caching does not address misrouted queries.

MREasy Which TWO describe a model cascade? (Select TWO)

A. A router sends simple requests to a cheap model and complex ones to a flagship model

B. It requires fine-tuning both models

C. It optimizes price-to-performance per request

D. It guarantees lower latency for all requests

E. It works only with batch inference

Correct: A, C. Complexity-based routing is the mechanism; quality per dollar is the metric.

B is wrong: no fine-tuning is involved. D is wrong: complex requests still take flagship time. E is wrong: cascades are a real-time routing pattern.

MRMedium Which TWO metrics should a team track to validate a cascade? (Select TWO)

A. Quality scores per route (small-model route vs flagship route)

B. Router escalation and misclassification rates

C. Total number of AWS regions used

D. The router's favorite color

E. Batch job completion times

Correct: A, B. Per-route quality proves the small model holds up where it is used; escalation rates prove the router classifies correctly.

C is wrong: region count is irrelevant to routing quality. D is nonsense. E is wrong: batch metrics belong to offline jobs, not a real-time cascade.

MRHard Which TWO scenarios are POOR fits for cascading? (Select TWO)

A. Every request genuinely needs flagship reasoning; traffic is uniformly complex

B. Request difficulty is unknowable before generation and the router guesses randomly

C. 90% of requests are simple lookups with verified equal quality on the small model

D. The small model is 10x cheaper with lower latency

E. Traffic is steady and predictable

Correct: A, B. A: no easy traffic means no savings, only added complexity. B: a router that cannot classify adds cost and misroutes without benefit.

C is wrong: this is the ideal cascade scenario. D is wrong: cheap and fast small models favor cascading. E is wrong: traffic shape affects the PT decision, not the cascade decision.

Questions: Topic 09, CloudWatch metrics

MCEasy A team wants near-real-time visibility into token spend and throttling for Bedrock, with minimal custom work. Which service should they use?

A. CloudTrail

B. CloudWatch metrics and alarms

C. A custom Glue and Athena pipeline

D. SageMaker Model Monitor

Correct: B. Bedrock emits Invocations, InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, InvocationThrottles, and latency to CloudWatch automatically: the managed, minimal-work answer.

A is wrong: CloudTrail is the audit plane, not metrics. C is wrong: heavy custom work for a near-real-time need. D is wrong: Model Monitor targets tabular ML, not GenAI token metrics.

MCMedium The dashboard shows OutputTokenCount tripled week over week while Invocations and InvocationThrottles are flat. What is the most likely cause?

A. A capacity shortage

B. Responses got longer: a prompt change removed length limits or raised maxTokens

C. More users signed up

D. The model was throttled

Correct: B. Flat invocations with spiking output tokens means longer responses per call: a prompt or maxTokens regression, not traffic or capacity.

A is wrong: capacity issues show as throttles, which are flat. C is wrong: more users would raise invocations. D is wrong: throttles are flat per the scenario.

MCHard Finance wants alerts on unusual GenAI spend without the team maintaining thresholds for every workload pattern. Which combination is most correct?

A. Static CloudWatch alarms on Invocations only

B. CloudWatch anomaly detection on token metrics plus AWS Cost Anomaly Detection

C. Daily manual invoice reviews

D. CloudTrail Insights on API calls

Correct: B. Anomaly detection learns normal patterns and flags deviations without manual thresholds; Cost Anomaly Detection covers the dollar side. Minimal maintenance, as requested.

A is wrong: static thresholds on invocations miss token-driven cost changes and need constant tuning. C is wrong: manual reviews are neither near-real-time nor low-effort. D is wrong: CloudTrail tracks API activity, not spend anomalies.

MREasy Which TWO are CloudWatch metrics emitted for Bedrock? (Select TWO)

A. InputTokenCount

B. InvocationThrottles

C. PromptAttackBlocked

D. S3BucketSize

E. EC2CPUUtilization

Correct: A, B. Token counts and throttle counts are core Bedrock metrics.

C is wrong: guardrail block counts are not among the four core metrics named in this domain. D and E are wrong: S3 and EC2 metrics belong to those services, not Bedrock.

MRMedium A cost spike investigation needs both the trend and the offending prompts. Which TWO form the right drill-down path? (Select TWO)

A. CloudWatch metrics sliced by model ID to find which model drives the spike

B. CloudWatch Logs Insights over model invocation logs to find the expensive prompts

C. CloudTrail to read prompt contents

D. Deleting old log groups to save cost

E. Increasing provisioned throughput

Correct: A, B. A narrows the spike to a model; B finds the specific prompts and responses behind it. Metrics to logs is the standard drill-down.

C is wrong: CloudTrail does not record prompt bodies. D is wrong: deleting logs destroys the evidence. E is wrong: capacity does not explain a cost spike.

MRHard Which TWO are common monitoring mistakes the exam tests? (Select TWO)

A. Using CloudTrail for token-spend monitoring instead of CloudWatch

B. Using SageMaker Model Monitor for GenAI text quality drift instead of Bedrock evaluations

C. Slicing metrics by model ID

D. Setting alarms on InvocationThrottles

E. Using anomaly detection for token bursts

Correct: A, B. Both are wrong-plane tools: CloudTrail is audit not metrics, Model Monitor is tabular ML not GenAI text. The exam offers both as distractors.

C is wrong: slicing by model ID is correct practice. D is wrong: alarming on throttles is correct. E is wrong: anomaly detection on token bursts is exactly the recommended approach.

Questions: Topic 10, Invocation logging and tracing

MCEasy A team must audit the exact prompts sent to a model and the responses received, for debugging a cost spike. Which should they enable?

A. CloudTrail data events

B. Bedrock model invocation logging to S3 or CloudWatch Logs

C. VPC Flow Logs

D. AWS Config rules

Correct: B. Invocation logging records request and response bodies: the prompt forensics plane.

A is wrong: CloudTrail records API calls, not prompt contents. C is wrong: flow logs show network traffic, not prompts. D is wrong: Config tracks resource configuration, not inference data.

MCMedium A multi-step agent averages 38 seconds per request. The team must determine whether the time goes to model calls or tool calls. What is the most direct approach?

A. Enable X-Ray tracing across the agent chain and read the segment timings

B. Increase provisioned throughput and see if latency drops

C. Check CloudTrail for slow API calls

D. Switch to a smaller model

Correct: A. Distributed tracing shows per-step timing: the direct measurement of where time goes.

B is wrong: adding capacity without knowing the bottleneck may optimize the wrong component. C is wrong: CloudTrail is audit, not timing. D is wrong: changing the model before measuring assumes the model is the problem.

MCHard A healthcare app logs model invocations to S3 for forensics. The compliance team flags the setup. What is the most likely issue and fix?

A. Logs are too verbose; disable logging entirely

B. Logs contain raw prompts that may include PII and are not encrypted; enable KMS encryption on the destination or restrict logging

C. S3 is the wrong destination; logs must go to CloudTrail

D. Invocation logging is not available for healthcare workloads

Correct: B. Invocation logs carry prompt and response bodies, which may contain PII. In regulated workloads the exam expects KMS encryption or disabled/restricted logging.

A is wrong: disabling forensics entirely is not the targeted fix. C is wrong: CloudTrail cannot hold prompt bodies. D is wrong: logging is available; it must be secured.

MREasy Which TWO do model invocation logs contain? (Select TWO)

A. The request body (prompt) sent to the model

B. The response body (completion) returned

C. The model's internal weights

D. Other customers' prompts

E. Real-time metric aggregations

Correct: A, B. Logs capture the full request and response for forensics.

C is wrong: weights are never exposed. D is wrong: logs contain only your account's invocations. E is wrong: aggregations are CloudWatch metrics, not logs.

MRMedium An agent intermittently gives wrong answers. Which TWO observability steps help diagnose it? (Select TWO)

A. Enable agent tracing (enableTrace) to see the reasoning steps and tool calls

B. Query invocation logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights to inspect the failing prompts and responses

C. Delete the agent and recreate it

D. Increase the provisioned throughput units

E. Disable all logging to improve performance

Correct: A, B. A reveals the reasoning path and tool sequence; B reveals the exact inputs and outputs of the failures.

C is wrong: recreation without diagnosis repeats the bug. D is wrong: capacity does not fix wrong answers. E is wrong: removing observability blinds the investigation.

MRHard Which TWO statements correctly distinguish the observability planes? (Select TWO)

A. CloudTrail records who called which API and when (audit plane)

B. Model invocation logs record prompt and response bodies (data plane)

C. CloudWatch metrics record prompt contents

D. X-Ray records API authorization decisions

E. Invocation logs and CloudTrail are interchangeable

Correct: A, B. The exam's core distinction: Trail is who-did-what, invocation logs are what-was-said.

C is wrong: metrics carry counts and timings, not contents. D is wrong: authorization is IAM/CloudTrail territory, not tracing. E is wrong: they answer different questions and are not interchangeable.

Questions: Topic 11, Token efficiency

MCEasy A chatbot resends the full 30-turn conversation history on every call. History averages 3,000 tokens. What is the simplest change that cuts input-token cost?

A. Window the history to the last 6 turns or summarize older turns

B. Increase the temperature

C. Switch to InvokeModel

D. Enable detailed monitoring

Correct: A. Context pruning directly removes input tokens from every call. It is free to implement.

B is wrong: temperature affects randomness, not tokens. C is wrong: the API does not change token counts. D is wrong: monitoring observes cost; it does not reduce it.

MCMedium After aggressive prompt compression, a summarizer's quality scores drop. The team compressed a 2,000-token instruction set to 200 tokens in one edit. What is the right recovery?

A. Restore the original prompt; compression never works

B. Re-expand selectively and re-evaluate at each step to find the smallest prompt that holds quality

C. Switch to a larger model to compensate

D. Increase maxTokens

Correct: B. Compression is an optimization loop: shrink, evaluate, stop when quality moves. One giant edit overshoots; iterate back up.

A is wrong: compression works when done incrementally with evaluation. C is wrong: a bigger model for a damaged prompt is the expensive wrong lever. D is wrong: output length does not repair instruction quality.

MCHard Token costs grow 30% month over month. Prompts include long histories, verbose instructions, and uncapped outputs. The CFO demands cuts without UX degradation. Which response is most correct?

A. Switch all traffic to the cheapest model immediately

B. Prune context, compress prompts, cap outputs, track tokens per feature, and re-evaluate quality after each change

C. Buy provisioned throughput

D. Move the workload to batch inference

Correct: B. The multi-lever answer: free prompt optimizations first, each verified against quality ("without UX degradation" demands re-evaluation).

A is wrong: a blind model switch risks the UX the CFO wants protected. C is wrong: capacity does not cut token-driven cost. D is wrong: the workload's interactivity is not stated as changeable. Batch is not a general cost fix.

MREasy Which TWO directly reduce billed tokens per call? (Select TWO)

A. Removing duplicate paragraphs from the system prompt

B. Setting maxTokens with concise-answer instructions

C. Raising top-p from 0.9 to 1.0

D. Enabling X-Ray tracing

E. Using a longer model ID

Correct: A, B. A cuts input tokens; B caps output tokens.

C is wrong: top-p controls sampling diversity, not token counts. D is wrong: tracing is observability overhead, not a token saver. E is nonsense.

MRMedium A RAG app stuffs 10 retrieved chunks into every prompt "to be safe." Which TWO changes improve token efficiency without hurting answer quality? (Select TWO)

A. Retrieve fewer, better-ranked chunks using hybrid search and reranking

B. Compress the instruction text around the chunks

C. Send all 10 chunks but lower the temperature

D. Disable chunk overlap entirely

E. Increase the embedding dimensions

Correct: A, B. A keeps the relevant context while dropping filler chunks; B trims the wrapper text. Both cut input tokens with quality checks.

C is wrong: temperature does not reduce tokens. D is wrong: overlap removal is a chunking-quality decision, not a guaranteed token win, and can harm retrieval. E is wrong: embedding dimensions affect storage and accuracy, not prompt token counts.

MRHard Which TWO are true about the relationship between token efficiency and the other cost levers? (Select TWO)

A. A leaner prompt multiplies the benefit of prompt caching, batch, and smaller models

B. Token efficiency should come before buying provisioned throughput

C. Token efficiency replaces the need for monitoring

D. Prompt compression eliminates the need for model evaluation

E. Token efficiency only matters for output tokens

Correct: A, B. A: every lever prices tokens, so fewer tokens amplify all of them. B: never reserve capacity for waste; prune first.

C is wrong: you still need metrics to prove the efficiency worked. D is wrong: compression requires evaluation; it does not replace it. E is wrong: input tokens usually dominate the bill.

Questions: Topic 12, Semantic caching

MCEasy A FAQ bot gets millions of questions with heavy repetition in varied wording. What minimizes cost and latency?

A. A semantic cache in front of the model with similarity matching

B. Provisioned throughput

C. A larger model

D. Longer system prompts

Correct: A. Repeated meanings are the semantic-cache use case: hits skip the model call entirely, cutting both cost and latency.

B is wrong: capacity does not eliminate repeated work. C is wrong: a larger model costs more per call. D is wrong: longer prompts cost more.

MCMedium After deploying a semantic cache, users occasionally receive answers to similar-but-different questions. What should the team tune?

A. Raise the similarity threshold and evaluate hit quality

B. Lower the similarity threshold to increase hits

C. Disable the TTL

D. Switch the cache from ElastiCache to S3

Correct: A. Wrong-but-similar answers mean the threshold is too loose. Raising it trades some hit rate for correctness, validated by evaluation.

B is wrong: lowering the threshold worsens the problem. C is wrong: TTL controls staleness, not similarity mismatches. D is wrong: S3 latency is wrong for a lookup cache and does not fix threshold tuning.

MCHard A personalized recommendation engine (every query is user-specific) is proposed for semantic caching to "cut costs 60%." Why will this fail?

A. Semantic caches cannot store personalized data

B. The hit rate will collapse because each query is unique; the cache adds complexity for no savings

C. ElastiCache does not support embeddings

D. Personalized queries are not allowed on Bedrock

Correct: B. Semantic caching lives on repetition. Unique-per-user queries never repeat, so the hit rate approaches zero. This is the exam's explicit rejection case.

A is wrong: caches can store anything; the issue is hit rate, not capability. C is wrong: the architecture can hold embeddings elsewhere; the economics still fail. D is wrong: no such restriction exists.

MREasy Which TWO distinguish semantic caching from prompt caching? (Select TWO)

A. Semantic caching can skip the model call entirely; prompt caching discounts tokens on calls still made

B. Semantic caching matches by meaning; prompt caching applies to a byte-identical static prefix

C. They are the same feature with two names

D. Prompt caching works without Bedrock

E. Semantic caching is a Bedrock pricing feature

Correct: A, B. Call elimination versus token discounting, and meaning-matching versus exact-prefix matching, are the two axes.

C is wrong: they are different mechanisms. D is wrong: prompt caching is the Bedrock feature; semantic caching is your architecture. E is wrong: reversed.

MRMedium Which TWO are valid cache-layer choices and their trade-offs? (Select TWO)

A. ElastiCache for sub-millisecond lookups at high throughput

B. DynamoDB for a serverless cache with no cluster to manage

C. S3 for the hot lookup path

D. CloudTrail as the cache store

E. The model's context window as the cache

Correct: A, B. ElastiCache optimizes lookup speed; DynamoDB optimizes operational simplicity.

C is wrong: S3 latency is unsuitable for a per-request hot path. D is wrong: CloudTrail is audit logging, not a cache. E is nonsense: the context window is per-request working memory.

MRHard A cached FAQ answer becomes wrong after a pricing change. Which TWO mechanisms keep the cache honest? (Select TWO)

A. TTLs that expire entries so fresh answers regenerate

B. Explicit invalidation of affected entries when source data changes

C. Raising the similarity threshold

D. Switching to a larger model

E. Disabling the cache permanently

Correct: A, B. TTLs bound staleness automatically; explicit invalidation corrects entries immediately on known data changes.

C is wrong: thresholds control match quality, not freshness. D is wrong: model size does not fix stale cache entries. E is wrong: it discards the savings instead of managing staleness.

Questions: Topic 13, Production operations

MCEasy A company runs an interactive chatbot, a nightly report job, and a steady API with a latency SLA. Which portfolio minimizes cost while meeting constraints?

A. Batch inference for all three

B. Streaming plus right-sized models for the chatbot, batch inference for the nightly job, provisioned throughput for the steady API

C. Provisioned throughput for all three

D. On-demand for all three with no caching

Correct: B. Each workload gets its matching lever: interactive gets streaming and right-sizing, offline gets batch, steady SLA gets PT. The portfolio answer.

A is wrong: batch latency breaks the chatbot and the SLA. C is wrong: PT for spiky chat and finite nightly jobs wastes idle hours. D is wrong: it leaves every optimization on the table.

MCMedium Outputs vary run to run and the contract requires 99.5% consistency on identical inputs. Which approach is most correct?

A. Buy provisioned throughput

B. Set temperature to 0, add deterministic caching, and version prompts

C. Switch to batch inference

D. Increase the model size

Correct: B. Consistency is controlled by sampling parameters (temperature 0), deterministic response caching, and prompt versioning. PT stabilizes latency, not randomness.

A is wrong: the classic conflation the exam tests. C is wrong: batch changes latency, not determinism. D is wrong: larger models are not inherently more deterministic.

MCHard A team must detect hallucinations in near real time and catch abnormal token spend, with minimal custom engineering. Which combination is most correct?

A. Bedrock evaluation jobs with LLM-based judgments plus CloudWatch anomaly detection on token metrics

B. A custom Glue and Athena pipeline over raw logs

C. Manual weekly review of sampled outputs

D. SageMaker Model Monitor plus CloudTrail

Correct: A. Managed evaluation jobs detect quality issues at scale; anomaly detection flags spend deviations. Both are managed, matching "minimal custom engineering."

B is wrong: heavy custom work for a near-real-time need. C is wrong: weekly manual review is neither near-real-time nor scalable. D is wrong: Model Monitor is tabular ML and CloudTrail is audit: wrong planes for both halves.

MREasy Which TWO belong in the "measure first" step of production operations? (Select TWO)

A. CloudWatch token metrics sliced by model

B. X-Ray traces for latency breakdowns

C. Guessing which prompt is expensive

D. Disabling all logging to reduce noise

E. Deleting old dashboards

Correct: A, B. Token metrics show cost by model; traces show where latency goes. Measurement before optimization.

C is wrong: guessing is what measurement replaces. D is wrong: it destroys the data. E is wrong: it destroys the visibility.

MRMedium A "token costs growing, CFO wants cuts without UX degradation" scenario appears. Which TWO make the response "most correct" rather than single-lever? (Select TWO)

A. Stacking multiple levers: prompt pruning, caching, cascading, semantic cache

B. Re-evaluating quality after each change to protect UX

C. Applying only prompt caching

D. Switching models without evaluation

E. Buying provisioned throughput as the cost fix

Correct: A, B. The exam rewards multi-lever answers plus quality verification: "without UX degradation" is a constraint the answer must satisfy, not just mention.

C is wrong: single-lever answers are the distractors. D is wrong: unevaluated switches risk the UX constraint. E is wrong: PT is a capacity tool, not a token-cost fix.

MRHard Which TWO orderings follow the optimization ladder correctly? (Select TWO)

A. Measure, prune the prompt, then consider caching, cascading, batch, and provisioned throughput

B. Skip model calls with semantic cache before discounting tokens with prompt caching

C. Buy provisioned throughput first, then measure whether it was needed

D. Move interactive traffic to batch inference before trying streaming

E. Optimize the prompt only after committing to a 6-month PT term

Correct: A, B. A is the ladder in order: free and general first, committed and specific last. B is the correct sub-ordering: eliminating calls beats discounting them.

C is wrong: committing before measuring reserves capacity for unmeasured waste. D is wrong: batch breaks interactivity; streaming is the interactive lever. E is wrong: prompt work is free and must precede capacity commits.
